posts.on_image: FACE THE SUN. I NEED THE LIGHT.
posts.caption: Every vacation picture my mother ever took was shot at high noon with the sun straight in our eyes. She had read the little sheet that came with the Kodak Instamatic, and it said bright light, so we got bright light. We'd line up in front of whatever lake we had driven eleven hours to see, and she'd back up, then back up some more, then tell us to quit squinting. Nobody could quit squinting. My little sister Peggy is crying in about half of them, and Dad looks like he's lifting a piano in the rest. Then the film went off to the drugstore, and two weeks later we got twelve pictures of the same five scrunched-up faces. She put every one of them in the album anyway.
posts.first:
We have a whole album from Lake of the Ozarks, summer of '66, and there isn't one pair of open eyes in it. Mom's thumb also turns up in the corner of every third picture like it was part of the family.

posts.on_image: EVERY KITCHEN HAD ONE CABINET YOU OPENED FAST AND SHUT FASTER.
posts.caption: Aunt Dottie threw a Tupperware party in the spring of 1971, and every woman on Maple Street went home with something in harvest gold. My mother bought the big cake carrier and a stack of bowls with the lids you had to burp. Within a year nothing in that cabinet matched anything else. You'd reach in for a bowl for the leftover green beans and half the lids in the house came out onto the linoleum. Mom would shove it all back with her knee and slam the door before it could change its mind. Somewhere in that pile there was a lid for every bowl. We just never found them on the same day.
posts.first:
Ours was the cabinet next to the stove. If a bowl went to a church supper, Mom put our last name on a strip of masking tape on the bottom, and she wanted it back. She checked.

posts.topic: Dad's tool chest vs Mom's butter knife drawer
posts.on_image: DAD'S TOOLBOX / MOM'S TOOLBOX / HERS FIXED MORE.
posts.caption: My dad had a red Craftsman chest in the garage with a drawer for every socket he ever owned, and he could tell from across the room which one was missing. My mother had the second drawer to the left of the stove. In it was a butter knife with a bent tip, a dime, a bobby pin, a roll of masking tape and a rubber band off the Sunday paper. With those she tightened every loose screw in the house, got the back off the transistor radio, and fished a stuck piece of toast out of the toaster (unplugged first, she wasn't crazy). Dad's tools came out for the big jobs, and the big jobs took all weekend. Hers came out on a Tuesday and were back in the drawer before the coffee finished perking.
posts.first:
I took that butter knife with me when I got married in 1979. It's still in my kitchen drawer, and it has outlasted two toolboxes and a whole socket set.

posts.on_image: WHAT DO I LOOK LIKE, A BANK?
posts.caption: On Saturday mornings you waited until Dad had his coffee and the sports page before you asked. You stood next to the recliner holding your glove so he'd know it was for something wholesome, and you said you needed a dollar for the Little League snack stand. He lowered the paper about two inches. Then came the question every kid in 1965 heard once a week, followed by a speech about caddying at the country club for a quarter a bag when he was your age. You stood there through the whole thing because you knew how it ended. He'd fold the paper, dig in his front pocket, and hand you two quarters and a look that said don't come back.
posts.first:
My dad kept his change in a Folgers can on the dresser and knew to the penny what was in it. I borrowed a dime once without asking, and he brought it up at supper.

posts.on_image: THE WISHBONE HAD TO DRY ON THE WINDOWSILL THREE DAYS. THOSE WERE LONG DAYS.
posts.caption: Grandma said a wet wishbone just bends, and a bent wishbone doesn't count, so after Thanksgiving dinner she rinsed it off and set it on the sill over the sink. Then nobody was allowed near it. My cousin Gail and I checked on it every morning before school like it was a science project. Grandma would tap it with one finger and say "Not yet." On Sunday she finally handed it over, one pinky each, no choking up, and she counted to three. I won, Gail said I cheated, and she has been saying it for fifty-some years.
posts.first:
I still set the wishbone on the kitchen windowsill every Thanksgiving. Grandma's rule stands. Three days, pinkies only, no choking up.
